stemMd: Why does a molten ionic salt conduct electricity whereas its solid crystal usually does not?

options.label: A
options.textMd: Solid salts contain no electrons or protons.

options.label: B
options.textMd: Melting destroys the charge on every ion.

options.label: C
options.textMd: The salt becomes a gas at the instant it melts.

options.label: D
options.textMd: Its ions can move through the liquid and carry charge.

options.label: E
options.textMd: The liquid produces new electrons from heat alone.

explanationMd: Charge transport requires mobile charged particles. In a crystal, ions are constrained to lattice positions; in the melt, they can migrate under an electric field. The distinction is mobility rather than the existence of charge.

distractorRationale.b: Removing ionic charge would not explain conduction.
distractorRationale.a: They contain charged particles, but the ions are not freely mobile.
distractorRationale.e: Mobile ions, not newly created electrons, explain conduction.
distractorRationale.c: Melting produces a liquid, not necessarily a gas.
